messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Vignette:
Linda is a 58-year-old North American woman who was widowed after her husband was killed in a car accident. When she speaks about what happened, the story comes out in fragments. She can describe the phone call telling her there had been a crash, the rush to get there, and then certain moments that feel brutally sharp: the sight of crumpled metal, emergency vehicles clustered on the road, and a heavy mix of smells that seems to have fixed itself inside her memory. At other times, when she tries on purpose to tell the event from beginning to end, she loses the thread and says it is strangely hard to reach, as if the memory will not come when she asks for it. What she does have are sudden returns of it, complete and immediate, set off by something outside her before she has any chance to prepare.

In the months after her husband’s death, Linda found that ordinary life had become full of moments that could turn without warning. If an ambulance siren sounded nearby, she felt her body tense before she had even consciously placed the noise. Seeing a car that had been hit, even in passing traffic or on the side of the road, could bring the whole scene back into her mind with a force that made the present moment disappear. She did not experience these reminders as distant thoughts. They arrived as if she were back in that emergency setting again, with the same sensory vividness, including the smell she associates with the scene. She has struggled to put words to that part, saying only that when the memory hits, she can smell what she smelled that day, and that this is one of the most unsettling aspects of it because it makes the event feel close and real rather than over.

She has become watchful in ways that shape her entire day. At home, especially at night, she repeatedly checks the doors and windows. She knows the house is usually secure, and yet she goes back to the locks again and again, unable to feel settled for long. What frightens her most is the sense that danger can appear suddenly and that she will be caught off guard. That same sense shows itself in her reactions to movement around her. If someone shifts unexpectedly nearby, she startles hard, reacting as though she is under immediate threat. The intensity of it embarrasses her, particularly in public spaces, and has made her feel exposed and unlike herself.

Sleep has become another battleground. Linda has trouble falling asleep, and when she does sleep she often wakes again, alert and unsettled. Nights seem to stretch around the rituals of checking the house and listening for sounds. By morning she is tired, and over time the exhaustion has narrowed her life further. She is unemployed, and the structure she once relied on has fallen away; days can become organized around managing the possibility of reminders rather than around plans or contact with other people. The anniversary of her husband’s death is especially difficult. As that date approaches each year, she becomes tense and preoccupied, already bracing for what she expects will come. On the day itself, even routine sights and sounds can feel charged. She has learned to dread that period, knowing how easily she can be pulled back into the worst moments.

Because the memory is so unpredictable, Linda has begun to mistrust her surroundings. A passing ambulance, a glimpse of collision damage on the road, even a smell that resembles the one fixed in her mind can undo her in an instant. Yet when she sits down and tries deliberately to remember in a controlled way, she often cannot. This contrast leaves her feeling shaken and confused. She has come to believe that the event is still too powerful for her mind to hold properly, that it lives outside her control and can break through at any moment. The result is a life lived in anticipation—of noise, of movement, of reminders, of nightfall, of the anniversary coming around again.

By the time she seeks help, Linda is worn down by the constancy of it. What finally brings her in is not one new event but the accumulation of years in which she has slept poorly, startled easily, checked the house over and over, and felt ambushed by memories she cannot summon intentionally but cannot keep away. She says she wants to know whether it is possible to be in the world without feeling that a siren or a damaged car will tear her back into that day. What she is most afraid of is that this will never loosen its grip, and what she is most hoping for is some way to feel safe in her own home and in her own mind again.
